title: Trump Trapped in Iran War With No Good Options as Sixth Month Begins
excerpt: The U.S. president faces a bind between accepting an Oman-brokered deal that grants Iran unprecedented Hormuz control or escalating a conflict that has failed to extract concessions from Tehran.
body:
• Trump's Iran war enters its sixth month with no viable path to the face-saving exit he promised would come by mid-April
  • An Oman-brokered interim deal could grant Iran supervision of the Strait of Hormuz — a concession Washington had vowed to prevent
  • Fresh airstrikes risk political fallout ahead of November midterm elections without improving prospects of forcing Tehran's hand
  • Global oil prices remain volatile, spiking as much as 7% during the latest exchange of attacks between the two sides

A Menu of Bad Options

As President Donald Trump's war against Iran enters its sixth month, this week's flurry of threats and stalled diplomacy has laid bare the ever-tighter bind he finds himself in, according to a Reuters analysis published Wednesday.

Trump is caught between two unappealing choices: accept an emerging interim deal, negotiated by Iran and Oman, that would effectively give Tehran supervision of the Strait of Hormuz it never possessed before the war — or follow through on warnings of sharp military escalation, risking a more prolonged crisis with no guarantee of better results.

"Trump has put himself in a box. Whether through military or diplomatic means, he doesn't look likely to gain much from Iran."

— Aaron David Miller, former Middle East negotiator for Democratic and Republican administrations

The Diplomatic Dead End

The contradictory signals from Washington and Tehran this week underscored the dysfunction. On Monday, Trump told reporters that talks were "going on right now" and called the discussions Iran's "last chance" to sign a deal.

Hours later, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei flatly denied any negotiations were taking place. All Iranian negotiators were in the country, he said, apart from Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, who was on a religious pilgrimage in Iraq. A senior Iranian source told Reuters no talks were planned.

Trump later called Iran's leadership "unbelievably duplicitous" on Truth Social, claiming Tehran had asked for a meeting — a characterization Iran has rejected.

Context and Background

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, initiating a conflict Trump initially predicted would last just weeks. More than five months later, the war has killed thousands, driven up U.S. gasoline prices, and dragged down Trump's approval ratings ahead of November's midterm elections, in which Republicans are fighting to maintain narrow congressional majorities.

A memorandum of understanding signed in June collapsed after renewed tit-for-tat strikes, with Trump declaring the interim agreement "over" after Iran targeted U.S. military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait.

Why Escalation Has Not Worked

The pattern has repeated multiple times: Trump threatens massive strikes, only to pull back. He has discussed with aides the possibility of targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, sending ground forces to seize its Kharg Island oil hub, and bombing a deep-underground nuclear site known as Pickaxe Mountain.

Most analysts agree that major escalation — short of a politically untenable ground invasion — would be no more effective than earlier bombing campaigns that killed senior Iranian leaders and damaged military capabilities but failed to change Tehran's posture, according to Reuters.

A U.S. official told Reuters on condition of anonymity that any temporary shipping arrangements would involve "no impediments" and no party overseeing transit — a characterization that appears at odds with what negotiators in the region have described.

Impact on Energy Markets and India

For global energy markets, the uncertainty has been punishing. Oil prices have spiked repeatedly during each flare-up, with the latest exchange pushing prices up around 7%. India, the world's third-largest oil importer, has been particularly exposed to the volatility, as have Indian diaspora communities dealing with elevated fuel costs in the Gulf, Europe, and North America.

Gulf states — home to millions of Indian workers — face their own precarious situation. Iran could emerge from the war with enhanced leverage over shipping lanes and regional stability, while Gulf countries shoulder the economic costs of an unresolved conflict.

What Comes Next

Trump could attempt to maintain the status quo — continuing a naval blockade of Iran's ports and periodically retaliating for attacks on shipping. But that approach offers no face-saving resolution to a conflict he had promised would end months ago.

With midterm elections approaching and his party's congressional majorities at risk, something will likely have to give. The question, analysts say, is whether Trump can accept a diplomatic outcome that falls far short of the total capitulation he once demanded from Tehran.
